Positive and negative indexing.simple: Index 0 se shuru hota hai, isliye a[0] pehla element hai. −1 se aakhri element milta hai, −2 se usse pehle wala.
Positive and negative indexing.pro: Indices are zero-based, and negative indices count from the end, so a[-1] is the last element and a[-len(a)] is the first. An index equal to the length is out of bounds and raises IndexError.

Rows and cells in 2-D.simple: 2-D array me pehla number row batata hai, doosra column. a[1, 2] ka matlab doosri row ka teesra column.
Rows and cells in 2-D.pro: For a 2-D array the first index selects the row and the second the column, so a[1, 2] is one scalar while a[0] is an entire row. Comma indexing is faster and clearer than chained brackets.

Fancy indexing with an index array.simple: List se index karne par kai elements ek saath milte hain — jaise a[[0, 2]] pehla aur teesra. Ye copy deta hai, view nahi.
Fancy indexing with an index array.pro: Integer-array indexing gathers the requested positions in the order given, and it always returns a copy. That copy is why writing into a fancy-indexed result does not modify the source array.

Index with a coordinate pair.simple: a[1, 2] me dono number alag-alag axis ke liye hain — row aur column — isliye result ek single value hota hai.
Index with a coordinate pair.pro: A coordinate pair indexes each axis independently and returns a scalar for a 2-D array. This is different from a[[1, 2]] which selects rows 1 and 2 along the first axis.

One index drops a dimension.simple: a[0] poore pehli row deta hai, aur us row ka apna shape hota hai — matrix ka shape kam ho jaata hai.
One index drops a dimension.pro: Basic indexing removes the indexed axis, so a (3, 4) array gives a (4,) row for a[0]. Keep the axis with a[0:1] when a downstream operation needs 2-D input.

Select a whole column.simple: Column lene ke liye row ki jagah colon lagate hain: a[:, 1] ka matlab 'saari rows, column 1'.
Select a whole column.pro: a[:, 1] keeps every row and fixes the column, returning a 1-D array of shape (rows,). Use a[:, 1:2] when the column must stay 2-D for broadcasting against a row.

Fancy indexing picks rows.simple: a[[0, 1, 0]] se rows chun sakte ho, aur wahi row baar-baar bhi le sakte ho — order aur repetition aapke control me hai.
Fancy indexing picks rows.pro: A list of row indices selects rows in exactly that order and may repeat them, producing a new first axis matching the list's length. The result is a copy of the selected rows, not a view.

take works along an axis.simple: np.take se kisi bhi axis par positions chun sakte ho — axis=1 likho to columns chunenge.
take works along an axis.pro: np.take(a, indices, axis=k) gathers along the named axis, which fancy indexing cannot express directly for axes after the first. It is the readable form for column selection by position.

Negative indices count from the end.simple: −1 aakhri, −2 usse pehle — count peeche se. Ye length badalne par bhi kaam karta hai.
Negative indices count from the end.pro: Negative indices resolve as length + index, so they stay correct when the array grows or shrinks. Going past -length raises IndexError rather than clamping.

Slice columns of a matrix.simple: Colon se 'sab' bolte hain, isliye a[:, 1] me saari rows aur sirf column 1 aata hai.
Slice columns of a matrix.pro: The colon preserves an axis and the number selects one position, so a[:, 1] returns a 1-D column. Mixing a slice with a scalar is the standard way to keep one axis while dropping another.

A boolean mask filters one dimension.simple: a[a > 5] me pehle True/False ka array banta hai, phir sirf True wale values chun liye jaate hain. Result chhota ho sakta hai.
A boolean mask filters one dimension.pro: Boolean indexing selects the cells where the mask is True and returns a 1-D copy whose length equals the True count. Because the shape can change, masks are for filtering, not for assignment of a fixed-shape block.

Index with paired row and column lists.simple: a[[0, 2], [1, 2]] me pehla list rows aur doosra columns batata hai — pairs bante hain: (0,1) aur (2,2).
Index with paired row and column lists.pro: Two index arrays broadcast position by position, so the result is a[(0,1)] and a[(2,2)], not a 2×2 block. That pairing is the most common source of surprising fancy-index results.

Rows, columns and single cells.simple: a[1] row deta hai, a[:, 1] column, aur a[1, 2] ek hi cell. Teen tarah ke selection, teen shapes.
Rows, columns and single cells.pro: The three forms answer different questions: a[1] is a row view, a[:, 1] a column view, and a[1, 2] a scalar. Printing .shape after each is the habit that keeps multi-axis code honest.

Ellipsis and newaxis.simple: Ellipsis (...) bachi hui saari axes ke liye hota hai, aur np.newaxis ek nayi axis add karta hai — broadcasting ke liye kaam aata hai.
Ellipsis and newaxis.pro: Ellipsis expands to every axis not named, which keeps indexing readable for 3-D and 4-D arrays. np.newaxis inserts a length-one axis, turning a (3,) vector into (1, 3) or (3, 1) to control how it broadcasts.
